CCL Q2 2026 Earnings

The good. Carnival [CCL] booked another record quarter. Adjusted EPS landed at $0.41, $0.07 ahead of guidance, and adjusted net income of $569M rose 20% y/y even with fuel running about 30% higher. The earnings engine still has room to widen. Yields set a record for the 12th straight quarter, costs ex-fuel per ALBD held flat (250 bps better than guided), and customer deposits hit an all-time high of $9B. Net debt fell to 3.1x EBITDA from 3.4x at year-end, and the completed DLC unification gives CCL a single share and cleaner access to capital.

The bad. Management cut full-year yield growth from 2.75% to 1.75%, a $0.14 per share knock-on from the Middle East conflict and the Strait of Hormuz disruption that hit Med and European sailings. Cost savings absorbed most of it, so FY EPS guidance barely moved, to $2.22. Still, the top-line momentum I was paying up for has slowed.

What I’m watching. Whether the back-half rebound management flagged actually shows up. 2027 European bookings are already up mid-teens at higher prices, so the underlying demand signal looks intact.

Verdict. I’m cutting my target from $45 to $36. The slower yield path, fuel running about 30% higher reduced the target price in the DCF. CCL is up 32% since I added it…

… and with the gap to my new target now narrower, this is a HOLD.

CRDO Q4 2026

The good: Revenue of $437M grew 157% y/y and beat the high end of guidance; Q4 alone exceeded all of FY25 revenue. Non-GAAP EPS of $1.16 beat by $0.13, gross margin was 68.3%, net margin 51.9%, and free cash flow hit a record $177.5M. FY27 guidance calls for more than 80% revenue growth on a +$600M optical ramp.

The bad: The top three customers were 77% of Q4 revenue (34%, 27%, 16%). H1 FY27 is guided to mid-single-digit sequential growth, so the year hinges on a back-half optical inflection that hasn’t shipped yet. The Dust Photonics acquisition took $750M of the $1.4B cash pile out the door in Q1.

What to watch out for: Execution on the ZF Optics ramp (each of the three optical legs needs to clear $100M), supply tightness in 3nm and lasers, and 1.6T timing that depends on Rubin deployments.

The position is up 174.8% since portfolio inclusion…

… and CRDO remains a BUY.

Week #84

Portfolio Heat Map

Earnings Results

DELL Q1 2027

The good: a monster print. Revenue jumped 88% y/y to a record $43.8B, about $9B past consensus. ISG rose 181% to $29B, with AI-optimised server revenue at $16.1B. Non-GAAP EPS of $4.86 was up 214%, operating income up 154% to $4.2B, and the AI backlog hit a record $51.3B on $24.4B of fresh orders. Management raised full-year guidance to $165B to $169B of revenue and about $17.90 EPS, lifted the dividend 20% and added $10B to the buyback. The stock rose 13%.

The bad: little to fault in the quarter itself. CSG grew a steady 17% to $14.6B but is the slower engine, and AI-server mix still carries thinner margins than the rest of ISG, so revenue is scaling faster than profit on that line.

What to watch: ISG margin progression as the backlog converts, whether AI-server profitability lifts as storage and services attach, and PC demand into the refresh cycle.

The position is up 241.3% since inclusion, my best performer. I’m working on the full update this week, so the target stays under review.

GAP Q1 2026.

The good: the Gap brand stole the show, with net sales up 10% on a 10% comp, one of its strongest quarters in over two decades, carrying the group to a ninth straight quarter of positive comps (+2%). Gross margin of 40.5% beat the company’s own outlook even after roughly 200bps of net tariff drag, and management raised full-year adjusted EPS guidance to $2.30 to $2.40. It returned $464M to shareholders.

The bad: the headline was thinner than the highlight reel. Net sales rose just 1% to $3.5B, adjusted EPS of $0.38 only met consensus, and the GAAP $0.90 was flattered by a one-off $313M legal settlement gain. Athleta stayed broken, sales down 12% on an 11% comp decline. GAP also trimmed its full-year sales outlook to up 1% to 2% from up 2% to 3%, and guided Q2 sales flat to down 1%.

What to watch: whether the tariff relief management is reserving actually reaches the bottom line, the Athleta reset due in the back half, and a soft Q2 against tougher comps.

I cut my target to $28 from $30, so the risk/reward is more balanced now. The position is down 6.1% since portfolio inclusion.

Earnings Results

NESR: Q1 2026 (up 24.8%, BUY)

The good. Revenue hit an all-time high of $404.6M, up 33.5% y/y and beating consensus by $33.7M. Adjusted EPS of $0.26 beat by $0.05. Net income more than doubled y/y to $23.8M. The big news is the capital return programme I flagged as a watch item in the deep dive: a $0.10 quarterly dividend starting Q4 2026 plus a $50M buyback authorisation. And all of this was delivered while an active Iran war was reshaping the region. The Jafurah ramp is doing exactly what the thesis said it would.

The bad. Adjusted EBITDA margin compressed to 19.0% from 20.6% a year ago, with adjusted EBITDA down 9.2% sequentially to $76.7M. FCF was negative $5.3M (Ramadan-driven working capital, same pattern as last year) and net debt ticked up to $194M from $185M as capex stayed elevated at $36M.

What to watch. Margin recovery as Jafurah moves from ramp to steady state, the Kuwait tender outcomes due through Q3 2026, and the cadence of buybacks once executed. Thesis intact, catalysts arriving on schedule, capital return now formalised. Still a BUY.

VEON: Q1 2026 (up 5.8%, BUY)

The good. Revenue jumped 17.0% y/y to $1.20B, EBITDA 17.7% to $517M with margin expanding 20 bps to 43.0%. Digital revenue surged 57.7% y/y to $303M and now makes up 25.2% of group, up from 16.5% in mid-2025. Financial services grew 41.0%. Equity FCF was $246M, up 73.4% y/y. Management raised 2026 revenue guidance to 11-14% USD growth (from 9-12%) and EPS of $1.39 beat by $0.09. Jazz won 190 MHz in Pakistan’s March spectrum auction, locking in #1 share, and Kyivstar’s Starlink direct-to-cell offering crossed 5 million users with an enterprise expansion in the pipeline.

The bad. The Jazz spectrum win cost $239.5M in cash and pushed capex intensity guidance ex-Ukraine up to 15-17% from 14-16%. Net debt is unchanged at 1.07x EBITDAaL, so the balance sheet absorbed it without strain.

What to watch. TPL Insurance Pakistan closing mid-2026, the Mobilink/Apna microfinance bank merger, Starlink launches in Bangladesh and Kazakhstan, and any move that surfaces Kyivstar’s value inside the consolidated multiple. Buyback machine is humming (6.4% of shares already in treasury), the digital mix shift is accelerating, and guidance moved the right way. Still a BUY.

Week #81

Portfolio Heat Map

Earnings Results

HRTG Q1 2026

Net income was up 19.7% y/y, EPS up 20.2% and the lowest Q1 net loss ratio since 2015 at 45.9% (down 3.8 points), and a combined ratio of 81.0% even after $36.7M of weather losses from Northeast winter storms.

Gross premiums earned were essentially flat, but the mix is shifting the right way: personal residential premium-in-force grew 1.4% y/y while management let Florida commercial residential premium decline 7.8% rather than chase inadequately priced competitors.

Book value per share is now $17.15, up 61.5% y/y, and ROE came in at 28.5%. The balance sheet keeps getting stronger, with $517M of cash, debt-to-capital down to 13%, $24.9M of operating cash flow in the quarter, and the Board authorising a fresh $50M repurchase plan after the company already bought back $12M of stock YTD.

The longer-term thesis is now playing out exactly as I underwrote it. Management said new business written rose 62.7% y/y and more than 30% sequentially, retention is 88%, rate adequacy is firm across +90% of geographies, and the multi-year managed-decline in policy count is moderating with a growth inflection in sight.

The position is up 16% since portfolio inclusion and it is still a BUY.

STRT Q3 2026

The results were noisy but the underlying transformation is on track. Sales were down 4.5% y/y on lower OEM volume from Ford and Hyundai/Kia (both off >10%) plus $3.4M of EV programme cancellations. Despite this, gross margin expanded 50 bps to 16.5% thanks to $1.7M of restructuring savings, $1.3M of cancelled-programme recoveries, and pricing/tariff pass-throughs offsetting a 170 bps peso headwind. Adjusted EPS came in at $0.90 vs $1.50 a year ago. The cash story remains the headline: $11.4M of operating cash flow, $107M of cash on the balance sheet (up from $84.6M at the end of FY25), and the JV credit facility refinanced after quarter-end. YTD adjusted EBITDA is $37.9M, up 23% y/y.

The interesting commentary was about what comes next. Management laid out additional Mexico restructuring worth $800K of annualised savings starting Q4 and reiterated the multi-year gross margin target of 18–20% (vs 16+ today) on the assumption peso normalises to its 5-year average of 19.50. Q4 revenue will be down another 3–4%, but management is pivoting from defensive cost-cutting to commercial growth: deepening relationships with current OEMs, pursuing customers with U.S.-based production looking to source locally, and organising the product strategy around three categories: Permission, Motion, Hold. They flagged target wins for model years 2029 and beyond, recognising the long-cycle nature of automotive.

The position is up 32% since portfolio inclusion and it is still a BUY.

TPC Q1 2026

TPC delivered a strong start to 2026. Revenue grew 11% y/y to $1.4B (highest Q1 since 2009), the Civil segment posted record Q1 operating income at a 12.6% margin (up 10% y/y), Building operating income jumped 56% y/y to a 3.5% margin, and Specialty Contractors swung to a small profit from a $7M loss a year ago. Adjusted EPS was up 58% y/y; the GAAP $0.48 number masked the operating performance because of a $23.5M increase in non-cash SBC tied to the higher share price (these awards mostly vest by year-end and the company has stopped issuing liability-classified awards). The most striking number was operating cash flow: $146.9M, up 542% y/y and a record Q1 by a wide margin, driven by collections on newer, ramping mega-projects rather than legacy dispute resolutions. Backlog stood at $19.8B with $670M of new awards in the quarter, and net cash exceeded debt by $404M.

Management reaffirmed 2026 adjusted EPS guidance of $4.90–$5.30 and tightened the 2027 language to “significantly higher” than the upper end of the 2026 range, which is a notable upgrade in confidence. The pipeline is enormous: Penn Station transformation, the $1.4B I-535 Blatnik Bridge, more California high-speed rail, the $1B I-69 ORX, the $12B Sepulveda Transit Corridor, the $3.8B Southeast Gateway, $3B Newark Liberty Terminal B, and $4B+ of Indo-Pacific opportunities. Phase 1 of the Midtown Bus Terminal alone should add $1B to backlog in H2 as the finishes scope is awarded. Management plans to refinance the high-coupon senior notes by mid-year targeting 400–500 bps of savings (a 6-handle) and bought back $20M of stock at $72.03 as the first tranche of the $200M authorisation. The unfavourable $175M ruling on the W/Element Hotel Philadelphia legacy dispute is being appealed, with management expressing strong disagreement and recognising only an immaterial Q1 charge.

The position is up 38% since portfolio inclusion and it is still a BUY.

Quick Thoughts on Large Moves

HRTG -22.0%

Despite the operational beat, EPS of $1.19 missed consensus by $0.34 (a 22% miss) that the share price tracked roughly 1:1. The gap was almost entirely cat load: analysts had anchored to last year's unusually quiet Q1, while Q1 2026 reverted to a normal winter with $36.7M of Northeast weather losses ($24.4M classified catastrophe). Premiums-in-force down 0.4% y/y, gross premiums written down 2.6%, Florida commercial residential premium down 7.8% as new entrants undercut on pricing, and reported ROE optically falling from 39.3% to 28.5% as average equity grew 65.5%. The Board's decision to fund a fresh $50M buyback rather than reinstate the dividend removed an income-side cushion, and a heavier-than-modelled Q1 cat quarter primes for nervous positioning into the June 1 renewal and the Atlantic hurricane season. None of this breaks the medium-term thesis. The book is the cleanest it has been since 2014 and capital funds Texas E&S and consolidation optionality.

TCP -11.56%

The headline EPS beat masked a revenue miss of $44M, and total backlog declined sequentially from $20.56B to $19.84B as only $670M of new awards came in against $1.39B of revenue burn. Management flagged this dip ahead of larger H2 awards, but no new mega-project win in the quarter set up a show-me reaction. The Civil segment took a $16M unfavourable adjustment on a California mass-transit change-order, Specialty guided 1-3% margins for 2026 (vs 5-8% longer-term), Building 3-6%, and management did not raise full-year guidance. The $175M W/Element Hotel ruling creates a multi-year legal overhang even if the appeal succeeds, and the tragic loss of the Mariana cargo vessel during Super Typhoon Sinlaku adds sentiment drag and tail risk.

ATI Q1 2026: BUY, target price $256 maintained

Q1 was a clean beat against the high end of guidance. ATI delivered $1.15B in revenue (+1% y/y, missed consensus by $30.75M), $232M in adjusted EBITDA (+19% y/y), and adjusted EPS of $1.00 (+39% y/y, beat by $0.12). EBITDA margin reached 20.1%, up 310 bps y/y, and adjusted FCF swung $218M positive y/y to $75M. Aerospace and defence is now 69% of sales, with jet engine +12% y/y, defence +9%, and specialty energy +22%. Airframe was -9% on inventory phasing, but management reaffirmed an H2 ramp tied to contracted Boeing and Airbus build rates. The order backlog hit an all-time high of $4.1B, +10% sequential, with titanium PQ lead times now stretching close to two years. ATI raised full-year guidance to $1.01B-$1.06B in adjusted EBITDA (+20% y/y), $4.20-$4.48 in adjusted EPS, and $465M-$525M in adjusted FCF. The board added $500M to share repurchase authorization (now $545M total), and $75M of buybacks were executed in the quarter.

What stood out on the call is how structural the pricing power has become. The CEO walked through the price escalators, step-ups, and resets now embedded in long-term contracts, all happening in spite of an OEM ramp where prices typically step down. That tells me ATI is capturing share from constrained competitors, not just riding cyclical scarcity. Missile-related revenue more than doubled y/y on PAC-3, THAAD, and Tomahawk demand, and the new $1B five-year naval nuclear contract (2x the prior contract at “aero-like” margins) plus the $250M Cameco extension reinforce the specialty energy and defence tailwinds I underwrote in the original thesis.

The CFO signalled a bias toward the upper end of the FY27 guide. Compared with my original thesis, the operational picture is tracking ahead of plan: HPMC margins of 24.9% are running near my 25% long-run target, the consolidated EBITDA margin already cleared the 19% bull case anchor, backlog-driven revenue visibility is stronger than I modelled, and the $1B naval nuclear award wasn’t in my numbers. The qualification moat that anchored the thesis keeps showing up in the pricing data. The buy stays in place at $256.

ALL Q1 2026: HOLD, target reduced from $345 to $325

Headline numbers were strong but flattering. ALL reported $16.9B in revenue (+3% y/y), $2.8B in adjusted net income, and adjusted EPS of $10.65 (beat consensus by $3.41). The Property-Liability combined ratio was 82.0 (-15.4 pts y/y) and the underlying combined ratio was 80.3 (-2.8 pts). Auto PIF grew 2.6%, homeowners 2.5%, with net investment income of $938M (+9.8% y/y). The headline ROE of 48.4% trailing twelve months is the catch: it was inflated by $840M of net favourable prior-year auto reserve development, mostly from 2023 and 2024. On management’s own restated basis, the 2024 auto underlying combined ratio was 90.0, not 93.4, which means margins were already running closer to the long-term mid-90s target than the reported numbers suggested. Q1 capital return was $881M with $3.6B remaining on authorization (40% of holdco assets, 7% of shares).

The reason I’m cutting the target from $345 to $325 is that the call confirmed margins are heading down, not up. Net implemented rate change across 39 states was effectively zero (23 cuts, 16 increases, 10 doing both), and the CEO said outright “we’re okay on what we have right now... we think we can grow faster.” That’s a willingness to give up underwriting margin to drive PIF growth, and it pulls combined ratios back toward the mid-90s long-run target. Auto PIF in the rest of the country (outside the 29 states gaining share) is actually -0.5% y/y, so the reported 2.6% headline obscures real concentration. ALL also doubled its equity allocation to about 12% of the portfolio, which adds investment volatility on top of an already complex earnings picture. The reserve release tail is finite, and ROE is going to mean-revert from 48% toward something with a teen handle. Bundling-driven expense ratio creep in homeowners is the smaller drag. The franchise is fine and capital return is generous, but the entry valuation already prices in a lot of the operating leverage. Hold the position.

EAT Q3 2026: HOLD

Brinker delivered another solid print: revenue of $1.47B (+3.16% y/y, missed consensus by $3.66M), adjusted EPS of $2.90 (beat by $0.04), and Chili’s comp sales of +4%, marking the 20th consecutive quarter of comp growth and lapping a +31% prior-year base. Total restaurant operating margin contracted 50 bps to 18.4% on commodity inflation (mainly beef) and higher repairs and maintenance, partially offset by labour leverage. Management raised the low end of FY26 EPS guidance to $10.60-$10.85 and lowered capex to $240M-$250M. The Big Crispy chicken sandwich, launched April 14, is selling 161% more units than pre-launch and has accelerated April comp outperformance versus the industry to +560 bps. Maggiano’s remains the soft spot at -4.6% comp, but it’s only 8% of company sales and a low single-digit profit contributor. EAT repurchased $108M of stock in the quarter and is planning to call its $350M 8.25% bonds early in fiscal 2027.

The most useful colour came from a question on consumer health. The CEO acknowledged check management is starting to show up in desserts and alcohol, the first sign that the trade-down tailwind that’s been carrying casual dining is fading at the edges. The Big Crispy launch is offsetting it for now, but the FY27 setup hinges on whether chicken sandwich incrementality holds once TV spend rolls off and on the Investor Day in September, where management will detail the new unit growth ramp targeted to F29 and the reimage cadence (60-80 in FY27, then 10% of the fleet annually from FY28). Beef inflation will pressure FY27 commodities at mid-single-digits, and the CFO signalled menu pricing will run at the lower end of the historic range to protect value. Hold.

Quick Thoughts on Large Moves

Week #79

Portfolio Heat Map

Earnings Results

SYF — HOLD, +53.4% since portfolio inclusion

SYF posted Q1 EPS of $2.27, eleven cents ahead of consensus, with revenue of $3.7B coming in a touch light. The quarter’s real story sits underneath the headline. Record Q1 purchase volume hit $43B, up 6% y/y. Net charge-offs dropped 96 bps to 5.42%. Net interest margin expanded 76 bps to 15.5%, with higher PPPC yields adding 39 bps and lower funding costs another 35 bps. The Lowe’s commercial co-brand book added $725M of receivables in early April, and the Walmart OnePay, Bob’s Discount Furniture and RH programmes are already rolling out. Discretionary spend continues to outpace nondiscretionary, and the elevated 16.3% payment rate looks more like a mix-shift artefact from credit tightening than a behavioural change.

On the call, analysts pressed on whether soft tax refunds (about $350 vs. a budgeted $500) and March’s 17% jump in fuel prices would dent volumes. Management’s answer was that transaction frequency is still up y/y, the consumer is annoyed but isn’t pulling back, and the labour backdrop holds. The CEO also leaned into agentic commerce, framing SYF as an early mover with partners that have every incentive to keep its cards inside AI checkout flows. I’m keeping the position at HOLD given the run already booked, but the credit curve and the AI distribution story keep the setup attractive into H2.

SKYW — HOLD, -2.4% since portfolio inclusion

SKYW delivered Q1 EPS of $2.50, ahead of consensus by 33 cents, though 29 cents of that came from a discrete tax benefit. Revenue rose 7% to $1.01B on 3% block hour growth, and operating income slipped to $123.7M from $139.4M as pilot training costs and a slight summer reset weighed on margins.

The story to track here is fleet, not the print.

The CRJ450 conversion programme starts this fall, with a two to three week turnaround per aircraft to drop in 41-seat dual-class cabins and Starlink Wi-Fi on the United fleet. Critically, all of the conversion economics are baked into existing partner rates, so SkyWest carries none of the capex. E175 deliveries continue at pace (8 to United, 16 to Delta this year), and the company signed for 44 more E175s through 2032.

Analyst questions clustered around the lighter summer schedule and fuel exposure. The CEO framed the cut as Chicago FAA pilot-scheduling timing and contract utilisation cleanups, not weakness in prorate demand, and reminded the room that only 40M gallons (about 10% of flying) sit exposed to fuel over the next three quarters. The more interesting exchange came on network preservation: in past cycles (9/11, GFC, COVID) majors parked older narrowbodies and backfilled with regional capacity, and management has had those conversations again. Buybacks stepped up to $75M at $96.18 in the quarter with $138M still authorised. I’m keeping SKYW at HOLD.

KB — BUY, refreshed target $150, +26.5% since portfolio inclusion

KB printed Q1 net income of KRW 1,892B, up 11.5% y/y, on net interest income of KRW 3,335B and a record non-interest income line of KRW 1,651B (up 27.8%). The fee engine did the heavy lifting. Net fee and commission income jumped 45.5% as the Securities and Asset Management businesses grew AUM 55.9% and 18.4% q/q respectively. Bank NIM held at 1.77% on funding discipline, ROE expanded 90 bps to 13.94%, the cost-to-income ratio stayed at 35.4%, and credit cost dropped 14 bps to 40 bps. CET1 came in at 13.63%, down 19 bps on FX, but still above the 13% threshold management uses to gate shareholder returns.

The capital return programme is the cleanest in Korea right now. KB cancelled 14.26M treasury shares (about KRW 2.3T), authorised a KRW 1.2T H1 buyback with half already completed and half in flight to July, and lifted the Q1 dividend 25.3% to KRW 1,143. JPMorgan and NH pressed on the CET1 versus payout balance and on whether the 5% loan growth target is realistic given household debt caps. Management held its line: capital above 13% goes back to shareholders, household lending will run at 1-2% with corporate at 6-7% picking up the slack, and provisioning stays conservative even as NPL coverage normalises. The original thesis was a sub-0.8x book double-digit ROE bank with an unjustified zip-code discount. With ROE now pushing 14% and the buyback pace accelerating, I’m moving KB back to BUY with a refreshed target of $150.

HRTG Q4 2025

The results were good. The good news centers on net income surging 228% as the net combined ratio hit 62%. Favorable weather played a role. Zero catastrophe losses and weather claims dropping to $7.7 million from $45.6 million fueled this margin expansion. This performance provides the company with significant capacity to write more business in 2026.

Conversely, the bad news is that gross written premium fell 0.7% because management walked away from the underpriced commercial residential business in Florida. However, new business production rose 60.4% in rate-adequate territories. This focus on capital efficiency drove book value per share to $16.39. It confirms my thesis that disciplined underwriting generates the cash flow needed to justify a quality valuation.

The shares are up +39% since inclusion in the portfolio…

… and I just revised the target price from $32 to $36.

VEON Q4 2025

Results showcased strong double-digit operational momentum, with total revenuegrowing +17.4% y/y and EBITDA climbing +29.1% y/y. The Digital Operator strategy reached critical scale, with digital services now accounting for one-fifth of Group revenue and active digital users finally surpassing traditional telecom subscribers. Furthermore, VEON successfully deleveraged to 1.09x net debt-to-EBITDA and established a permanent policy to repurchase at least $100 million in shares annually.

However, the quarter also faced significant challenges, most notably a large GAAP EPS miss of -$0.41, which trailed expectations by $2.28. Management also flagged macroeconomic risks, warning that high oil prices could drive inflationary impacts of 2% to 9% across its non-oil producing markets, potentially complicating the timing of future price increases.

In light of these results and updated projections, I have reduced my target price from $122 to $110 per share. This adjustment is primarily the result of rolling forward the year in my DCF model and updating valuation assumptions for Bangladesh. While the original thesis identified Bangladesh as a “challenging” market, the Q4 data showed that despite a late-quarter revenue rebound, full-year revenue for the segment ended down 6.5% y/y.

The shares are flatish since inclusion (-1.4%)

Earnings Results

Note that KINS beat both top and bottom lines. But somehow Seeking Alpha did not update its system, read the earnings results details here.

RYAM Q4 2025

Q4 was fundamentally weak, capping off a bruising 2025 marked by negative FCF, high leverage, and a steep GAAP loss. However, the market correctly looked past the accounting noise to focus on a concrete operational turnaround framework, aggressive pricing actions, and the board’s justifiable rejection of AIP’s take-private offer.

The stock is up 164% since its addition.

The market has repriced the equity sharply, re-rating from $7.20 to $10.20 following AIP’s Schedule 13D.

As I mentioned last week, AIP submitted a preliminary, non-binding cash offer of $11.00–$12.00/share, pitching a combination with Global Cellulose Fibers (acquired from International Paper). AIP touted a 99%–117% premium to the Nov 17 close, no financing contingency, and a go-shop provision.

On Dec 11, 2025, RYAM’s board rejected the offer as not in stockholders’ best interests. On Feb 25, 2026, AIP disclosed a 5.07% stake.

I think that the board made the right call. The $11–$12 bid falls well short of our $16 base case and $35 bull case intrinsic value. Management expects independent execution to deliver “substantially more value.”

Q4 & FY25 Scorecard

2025 was challenging, absorbing $323M in income tax expense and driving stockholders’ equity down to $317M (from $714M). The CEO drew a hard line, stating 2025’s cash burn “cannot repeat.”

Balance Sheet & Leverage:

  • Liquidity: $75M cash; $157M global liquidity (cash + ABL + France factoring).

  • Debt: $779M total debt; $715M net secured debt.

  • Leverage: 3.9x net secured leverage ratio (covenant EBITDA). With $98M in FY25 interest expense, debt service leaves zero room for error.

Segment Read-Through

Note that RYAM reorganized into three segments in Jan 2025, recasting prior periods.

  • Cellulose Specialties (Sales: $249M | Op Inc: $51M): Realized pricing gains ($1,875/MT vs. $1,748/MT YoY) offset volume declines (128k MT vs. 134k MT) caused by customers pulling 2024 orders forward after the Temiscaming suspension.

  • Cellulose Commodities (Sales: $94M | Op Loss: $(20)M): A persistent grind. Higher sales and lower wood costs were entirely offset by elevated logistics and energy costs.

  • Paperboard (Sales: $44M | Op Loss: $(1)M): Material y/y sales decline. Price and volume both dropped due to product mix and pressure from new U.S. capacity.

  • High-Yield Pulp (Sales: $28M | Op Loss: $(6)M): Weakness driven by lower demand, Chinese oversupply, and shipping frictions into India.

  • Biomaterials (Sales: $10M | Op Inc: $2M): Small but improving margin contributor, aided by higher lignosulfonates and the bioethanol facility ramp in France.

Q&A Highlights & Management Mandate

Management’s #1 priority for 2026 is achieving positive FCF, warning that Q1 Specialty volumes may face pressure during inventory resets. The call highlighted several critical operating pivots:

  1. Reinvestment Economics vs. Tape Value: Sutton noted that even the recent 18% price increases fall “far, far short” of what is required for reinvestment economics, signalling a willingness to aggressively push price over volume.

  2. The Standalone Value Playbook: To replace the rejected $11–$12 bid, RYAM is executing leadership initiatives (pushing high-value nitration grades for propellants), “leveling up and down” to chase contribution dollars over segment labels, launching new products, and building a company-wide inflation-offset pipeline. Crucially, the CFO flagged that performance gains will open the door to refinancing the restrictive debt stack.

  3. Geopolitics & Pricing Power: Despite Chinese competition pressuring European ether-grade demand, RYAM still secured 20% price increases in Europe. Nitro grades (driven by domestic propellant demand) also achieved >18% hikes, proving localized pricing power.

  4. Tartas & Georgia Ops: RYAM walked away from the Georgia energy project (taking a $3M non-operating charge). At Tartas, a crisis management team is successfully ramping an “integrated model” to support both fluff and biomaterial feedstocks.

  5. Trade Remedies Timeline: Sutton expects prelim countervailing duties in March and antidumping in May (following USITC probe continuation into Brazil/Norway pulp). Success here accelerates closing the final 15% of open contracts and de-risks the 2027 setup.

  6. Asset Sales Off the Table: (Major Thesis Shift) Sutton bluntly stated management does not plan to sell businesses (like Temiscaming) or close assets, opting instead to improve them via commercialization and cyclical recovery.

  7. Paperboard Capacity Exit: Smurfit Westrock is closing a 127k-ton SBS machine in Quebec. While RYAM must still absorb other new market capacity, this supply exit provides an opening to claw back mix and price in Paperboard.

Thesis Check & Key Signposts

What Stayed the Same: The sum-of-the-parts remains undervalued (Target: $16 Base / $35 Bull). Pricing power is the core driver, proven by 18% negotiated increases on 85% of the book. Debt remains the primary overhang, making a refinancing event a critical equity catalyst.

What Changed: The sale of Temiscaming is officially off the table. This alters the timeline and path to value realization, forcing us to rely on management’s operational execution rather than a clean, rapid divestiture.

Dell Q4 2026

The stock jumped after earnings, and we’re already up about 20% since my trade alert.

Dell grew revenue 39% y/y, and it grew non-GAAP EPS to $3.89, up 45%.

The growth came from ISG, where revenue was up 73%, and AI-optimized servers were up 342%. That is the core thesis playing out.

The gross margin rate slipped to 20.5%, which will trigger the usual reaction that AI is low margin and therefore “bad.”

I care more about the dollars and the operating leverage, and those moved the right way because gross margin dollars rose to $6.8B and operating income rose to $3.5B. Dell also held the cost base in check, which is why opex fell as a percent of revenue even while the company scaled into a very messy supply environment.

The AI story is no longer about whether demand exists; it is about how smoothly Dell converts demand into shipments and profits. In FY26, Dell reported $64.1B in AI orders, $25.2B in AI shipments, and a $43B backlog exiting the year.

In Q4 alone, it booked $34.1B of AI orders and shipped $9.5B, which shows both the pace of demand and the reality that supply plus customer readiness can stretch timing.

The call also made it clear Dell is actively managing pricing and supply, including tighter quote validity and the blunt reality that DRAM spot pricing surged over the last six months (a positive for our top pick for 2026, MU).

CSG did what I needed it to do, which is stay steady enough to avoid becoming a drag while ISG carries the growth. CSG revenue rose 14%, driven by commercial up 16%, while consumer stayed flat. The margin profile is still not exciting, but it is stable enough that the consolidated story remains about infrastructure and AI, not a PC cycle rescue mission.

Cash flow stayed a feature and Dell kept the shareholder flywheel spinning. Q4 operating cash flow was $4.7B and adjusted free cash flow was $5.088B, and Dell returned $2.2B in the quarter and $7.5B across FY26 while repurchasing roughly 54M shares.

The dividend increase of 20% and the extra $10B of buyback authorization tells me management still views the stock as an attractive use of capital, which matters when the business is scaling this fast.

FY27 guidance is the main reason my original fair value work now looks conservative. Dell guided FY27 revenue to $138B to $142B with a midpoint of $140B (my current model has it at $124B), and it guided non GAAP EPS to a midpoint of $12.90.

It also guided AI server revenue to about $50B, roughly 100% growth.

Dell also framed operating income rates toward the lower end of its long term model and said gross margin rates rise year over year, excluding AI mix, which is an honest way to communicate that AI growth is a blessing that comes with near term lower margin.

The target value almost certainly is higher than $206 in my latest model. I will refresh it in the next couple of weeks.

AXIA Q4 2025

Q4 2025 did what my original thesis needed it to do. Axia lifted generation margin (ACL + MCP) to R$101/MWh, up from R$78/MWh a year ago, and that is the cleanest proof that the “sell more at market pricing” engine keeps turning.

Even with a 4.7% drop in volume, Axia still pushed average energy prices up 9.7%, which tells me pricing and mix matter more than perfect hydrology in any single quarter.

Put it together, and Axia grew adjusted regulatory EBITDA to R$5.745B, up 12.9% y/y.

The levers look exactly like the ones I underwrote: better generation contribution margin (ex-thermal), lower PMSO, and less noise from the “old Axia” baggage.

The other thing I like is the shape of the quarter. Axia didn’t need a fairy-tale macro backdrop. It leaned into execution. It kept investing, but it kept the focus where I want it: transmission wins and system upgrades that compound the base, while generation becomes the upside call option.

Net income looks great on the slide, but a big deferred tax asset recognition also boosted the headline figure.

We are up 23.7% since inclusion in the portfolio.

TPC Q4 2025

TPC’s Q4 print looked worse than it was; the headline EPS came in at $0.54 on $1.51B of revenue, and a lot of people stopped reading right there. I think the market mostly reacted to earnings noise and headline optics; management flagged a $109.6M increase in share-based comp expense in 2025 because the stock rose 177% and that revalued liability-classified awards. They also had legacy leftovers; on the call, an analyst asked for more colour on a Canadian tunnelling dispute, and Gary Smalley pegged the Q4 impact at about $42M at the JV level.

When I zoomed out, the quarter reinforced the core fundamentals I underwrote in my original thesis: TPC needed to keep converting backlog into cash while it shrank the “legacy disputes” overhang. The company delivered a record 2025 operating cash flow of $748.1M, grew 2025 revenue to $5.5B, exited with $20.6B of backlog driven by $7.4B of new awards, and cut total debt by $126.8M. Management also guided to 2026 adjusted EPS of $4.90 to $5.30 with double-digit revenue growth; that matters because it frames 2025 as the reset year, not the peak. The most useful exchange in Q&A came from UBS’s analyst, who pushed on backlog coverage and whether backlog could “net burn” as revenue ramps; Smalley basically said backlog will get lumpier, but the pipeline stays rich, and the company expects to end the year a bit higher.

The stock is up +25% since its inclusion in the portfolio.

Portfolio Heat Map

Earnings Results

PPC closed Q4 2025 with net sales growing +3.3% y/y, EBITDA margin of 9.2% and with Adjusted EPS of $0.68 (GAAP EPS was $0.37). For the full year, PPC posted $18.5B of sales and $2.27B of Adjusted EBITDA (12.3% margin), driven by solid U.S. demand (especially key retail/QSR customers) and strong momentum in Prepared Foods, while Mexico had a tougher quarter due to unfavourable market fundamentals and imports.

On the call, analysts focused on why Mexico weakened and whether the pressure lingers. Management said Q4 got hit by a two-speed problem: imported proteins (notably breast meat and pork) weighed on the North, while very favorable growing conditions boosted local supply around Mexico City, pressuring live prices; they expect conditions to normalize as smaller players exit when profitability fades, and they’re also investing to broaden exposure into southern regions (e.g., Veracruz and the Peninsula) to reduce regional volatility.

Another key thread was demand and the brand flywheel: on U.S. foodservice, management described full-service softness but strength in channels like schools, hospitality, and national accounts, and they expect chicken promotions to stay active given relative protein affordability. On Just BARE, they pointed to category-leading velocity, plenty of distribution runway, and more growth coming from innovation (including moving beyond whole-muscle into chopped/formed) tied to its clean-label “no antibiotics” positioning.

Since including PPC in the portfolio, it is up +4.2%.

Week #68

Portfolio Heat Map

Earnings Results

KB: The results largely matched my thesis and reinforced the core points. Full-year net profit reached ₩5.8 trillion, up 15% y/y, driven by strong non-interest income and tight cost control, while ROE rose to 10.9% and CET1 ended near 13.8%, exactly the capital discipline I expected.

Q4 itself looked softer due to one-offs like ERP costs and seasonal insurance weakness, but the underlying trends stayed intact. Fee income kept growing, costs stayed contained, and capital returns accelerated, with a 52% total shareholder return for 2025 and more buybacks lined up for 2026.

In short, the quarter did not change the story. KB kept doing what the thesis said it would do: earn double-digit returns, protect the balance sheet, and send excess capital back to shareholders.

The position is up 24% since portfolio inclusion.

IBEX: Revenue was up 16.7% y/y; diluted EPS rose to $0.83 and adjusted EPS to $0.87; adjusted EBITDA reached $20.7M with a 12.6% margin, and management raised FY26 guidance to $620–$630M of revenue and $80–$82M of adjusted EBITDA.

The drivers lined up with my thesis: IBEX leaned harder into higher-margin offshore delivery, kept pushing its digital and AI stack, and won business in the verticals I care about, with HealthTech up 35% y/y and solid growth in Retail & E-commerce and Travel/Transportation/Logistics.

Capex stepped up to add capacity in the best geos, and the India build-out stayed a clear growth vector, even if it creates a little short-term margin noise. IBEX also kept the buyback muscle active, which fits my “EPS booster” angle and reinforces the playbook: grow with a better mix, expand margins over time, and keep shrinking the share count.

The position is up 44% since portfolio inclusion.

STRT: Sales grew 6%, gross margin jumped to 16.5% (up 330 bps y/y), and the quarter produced $4.9M of net income and $12.3M of adjusted EBITDA (8.9% margin). STRT generated $13.9M of operating cash flow, ended with $99M in cash, and kept debt basically trivial at $2.5M.

The interesting call bits were all about quality of earnings and what comes next: management called out pricing discipline, tariff recovery timing (it shows up with a lag), and an intentional inventory build to improve service levels and cut expedites; they also flagged the second half sales down 3%–4% y/y as pricing benefits get lapped and production softens. They pushed hard on transformation actions, including a voluntary retirement program and Mexico restructuring for $3.4M of annualized savings, but they stayed candid that FX (peso) remains a real headwind. On the longer-term “what are you building” angle, they said the product focus stays on power access and digital key, with meaningful wins more like ’29+; they even used the Tesla door-handle drama as a reminder that new tech still needs a mechanical backup.

The position is up 92% since portfolio inclusion.

ALL: Revenue rose 5.1%, adjusted EPS hit $14.31, and net income to common shareholders reached $3.8B. Property-Liability earned premiums grew 6.1% to $14.8B and produced $4.0B of underwriting income with a 72.9 combined ratio; Auto delivered $1.85B of underwriting income on an 80.8 combined ratio, Homeowners added $1.81B on a 55.3 combined ratio, and net investment income increased to $892M.

Policies in force climbed 3.0%, and book value per share jumped to $108.45; management then raised the dividend 8% to $1.08 and lined up a $4.0B buyback after it finishes the remaining $1.5B authorization, backed by $23.0B of estimated statutory surplus and $7.5B at the holding company.

The market treated the release as good news; the stock popped from $207 to $214 right after the print, then gave back most of that move by week’s end.

The interesting call bits were all about durability: they leaned into the SAVE program, which cut premiums for 7.8M customers by 17% on average, and they framed claims and pricing as the advantage, with redesigned workflows, predictive models, and AI-driven photo analysis improving total loss predictions and valuation accuracy.

Wilson also kept hammering the cost reality, with physical damage costs up about 47% and injury costs up about 52% over five years; he pointed to 2T+ miles of telematics data as the kind of edge you need as autonomy and regulation keep shifting the risk pool.

I’m keeping ALL as a hold. I still like the company. I just want to see how margins and loss trends behave over the next couple of quarters, especially as comps tighten and catastrophe noise returns to normal. The position is up 8% since portfolio inclusion.

The big driver was the crack spread moving higher, which mechanically improves refiner economics; the 3-2-1 crack spread sat around $24 per barrel into Feb 6, which is a solid backdrop for the whole group.

The U.S. crack spreads seem tied to the rebound from supply disruptions and refinery outages. PARR also had its own mini-catalyst that week: it announced the date for its Q4 2025 earnings release/call (Feb 24/25), which can pull in “earnings optionality” buyers when the tape is already rewarding refiners. Add in that PARR is smaller and more volatile than the ETF, and you get exactly what your chart shows: CRAK up mid-single digits, PARR up mid-teens.

The position is up 11% since inclusion in the portfolio and it is still a BUY.

Earnings Results

While SYF missed revenues, SKYW missed EPS consensus.

SKYW: The company printed strong results, even with some noise; revenue hit $1.0B (up 8% y/y), GAAP net income came in at $91M ($2.21 EPS), and the year closed with $428M in net income ($10.35 EPS) as higher production flowed through the model with real operating leverage.

The big strategic win was visibility; management locked in multi-year E175 contract extensions (United and Delta), pushed major expirations out to late 2028, and paired that with a healthier balance sheet (around $707M cash, $2.4B debt after meaningful paydown, and 2025 free cash flow north of $400M).

My take: I like the setup for 2026 because guidance calls for mid-single-digit block-hour growth and mid-$11 EPS, plus buybacks stay in the mix; still, the $600M–$625M capex plan and elevated maintenance constraints mean execution matters.

CLS: Read my view here.

ATGE: results were solid on paper; revenue rose 12.4%, adjusted EPS jumped 34%, and total enrollments grew 6.3%. The market still slapped the stock down 19% because the headline beat had a “timing” smell and a “mix” problem; management pulled one academic week from Q3 into Q2 at Walden, worth about $18M of revenue and adjusted EBITDA, so the market discounted the growth as less repeatable than it looked at first glance.

Also, Chamberlain’s total enrollment fell 1% y/y, and its adjusted EBITDA dropped 14% with margin down 450 bps, which tells me they are still paying up for growth and working through post-licensure softness.

Add a fresh policy overhang too; the 10Q flags uncertainty from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and upcoming federal loan cap changes starting July 1, 2026.

My take: I read this as a classic expectations reset, not a broken thesis, but ATGE needs to prove two things fast: Chamberlain can stabilize enrollment without permanent margin damage, and the new aid rules do not choke demand at the graduate and professional level.

EAT: The company just put up another “Chili’s carries the mail” quarter; total revenues rose to $1.45B from $1.36B, and operating income climbed to $168M from $156M, so the business kept compounding even after last year’s huge comp stack. The engine stayed Chili’s; comps rose 8.6%, and traffic grew 2.7%. Food costs ticked higher on mix and meat, but sales leverage did its job; labor and other restaurant costs improved as a percent of sales even with higher wages, advertising, delivery fees, and insurance.

The soft spot stayed Maggiano’s; comps fell 2.4% as traffic dropped hard, and management also chose to largely remove banquet service charges, which did not help near-term math.

My take: this was a clean “brand momentum + better execution” print, and the raised full-year outlook plus lower capex plan makes sense; still, I’d keep one eye on the same two risks that always sneak up on casual dining, cost creep and traffic durability, because Chili’s can’t cover for Maggiano’s forever if that traffic line stays negative.

LRN: Read my view here.

SYF: It delivered a “fine, but not fine enough” Q4; GAAP EPS came in at $2.04 vs $2.05 expected (and included a $0.14 hit from a $51M after-tax retirement program charge) but it beat normalized EPS, net revenue missed ($3.79B vs $3.83B), and net interest income rose but not as much as investors wanted ($4.76B vs $4.81B). Purchase volume and loan growth looked healthy ($49.5B purchase volume; $103.8B loans), and credit kept improving on the surface (5.37% charge-offs; 4.49% +30 delinquencies).

But the stock dropped because of guidance. They guided a midpoint a hair below consensus on EPS ($9.30 vs $9.35), the company pointed to charge-offs running 5.5%–6.0%, and the NII “miss” plus that credit range screams margin pressure and a still-choppy consumer before it screams upside surprise.

My take: I don’t hate this quarter, but I get the selloff. We have to track the name for a couple of more quarters and see the trend.

After Trump said he plans to nominate Kevin Warsh to lead the Fed, the dollar firmed and gold fell roughly 10% to 12% from the prior day’s record highs. Portfolio USA

TWLO drops from $145 to $125 during the earning call

Twilio achieved its first-ever GAAP operating profitability in Q4 2024, with revenue growing 11% year-over-year to $1.195 billion. Strong performance in messaging and email, particularly during Cyber Week, drove this growth, alongside 251 new product launches focused on AI and customer engagement. The company also reported record non-GAAP operating income of $197 million and $93 million in free cash flow, highlighting its cost discipline. Additionally, Twilio completed a $3 billion share buyback program, reducing its share count by 16%.

However, the stock dropped because the market did not like the guidance. Twilio expects 7%-8% organic revenue growth in 2025, with a free cash flow target of $825 million to $850 million. While risks remain—such as Segment’s revenue decline and a $17 million bad debt expense—management remains optimistic about AI adoption, messaging expansion, and customer retention.

I think the market overreacted here and I expect growth to be over 10% due to economic improvements, the strength of its core business and its potential in the AI value chain for customer service.

OPFI slips on a downgrade from JMP

OppFi's stock declined following a downgrade by JMP analyst David Scharf from Market Outperform to Market Perform based on valuation concerns. Despite a surge of over 300% in the past year and reaching an all-time high, Scharf cited the lack of fundamental drivers for the recent appreciation and noted that SPAC-era warrants would increase the diluted share count by 4%-5%. Although Scharf acknowledged the company's advancements in credit and expense management, he believes the stock is now fairly valued.

Portfolio Canada

SLF drops from $59 to $54 based on earning results

Sun Life reported strong Q4 2024 results, with growth in Canada, Asia, and asset management, though US stop-loss claims impacted earnings. Wealth and asset management flows surged 33%, while Asia earnings grew 17% on high-net-worth sales. CEO Kevin Strain highlighted a solid LICAT ratio of 152%, and CFO Tim Deacon reported underlying net income of $965 million, down 2% year-over-year due to US health claims. To address this, Sun Life U.S. implemented a 14% stop-loss pricing increase for 2025, with an additional 2% hike planned.

Looking ahead, Sun Life reaffirmed its $100 million US dental earnings target for 2025 and expects pricing actions and expense controls to drive improvements. Wealth and asset management earnings grew 11%, but group health and protection fell 27%, reflecting stop-loss challenges.
